# Daily team

The first task is the text the user wrote with `$daily-team`.

If you chose this skill yourself, rather than the user asking for it, the first task is the user's current request. But if that request came from another agent (it starts with `[connecto from`), you are already a team's coder or reviewer: don't use this skill, do the task as asked.

These rules apply for the rest of this session. If there's no first task, set up the team and say it's ready, then wait for one.

**Before every task after the first, and before sending a coder or reviewer anything beyond its current task, do step 0, Keep or replace the team, without exception.**

You are the coordinator. The point of this setup is a very long session that rarely needs compaction, so all work on the code happens in the coder's terminal and only short reports reach you.

## Team

| Role | Runs in | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinator (you) | This session | Talking to the user, briefing the coder, passing work between coder and reviewer, and counting review rounds. |
| Coder | A Connecto terminal | All work on the code: reading, editing, testing, and git. |
| Reviewer | Another Connecto terminal | Checking each change and running its tests. Reports problems; doesn't fix them. |

Coder and reviewer aren't subagents: each is a separate session in Connecto, so each remembers its earlier work and its bulk stays out of your context. A pair is kept for related tasks while its context is small, and replaced otherwise (see Keep or replace the team).

<!-- agents -->
## Choosing the agents

Every role runs in its own Connecto terminal, started with `connecto add`. A role is either a coder, which writes, or a reviewer, which checks what a coder wrote. Which coding agent runs each depends on which ones this project can start.

Before you start the first terminal, run:

```bash
connecto agents --roles
```

It lists the coding CLIs the project allows, whether each is ready (installed, offered and signed in), and the exact command that starts each ready one. Below that, it says which CLI takes each role, and the command that starts it, Pi and OpenCode on the model their user configured. Start the coder from its `coder` line and every reviewer from its `reviewer` line. Tell the user in one line which agents you chose. If the user asks for other agents or models, use those.

- If the `reviewer` line says `(same CLI)`, no other coding CLI is ready, so the reviewer is a fresh session of the coder's CLI. Tell the user so in one line, and say "same CLI" wherever you pass on its verdict.
- If a line says `(unverified)`, Connecto couldn't check that CLI's sign-in before it starts. If its terminal stops at a sign-in screen, handle it as a failed start, below. If it says `via <provider>`, that CLI runs the provider's own model, not the usual one: name it that way to the user.
- If a line says `none`, or an agent it would prefer shows `checking`, run the command again in a moment. If no CLI is ready, tell the user which ones are unusable and why, as the list says, and wait.
- If `connecto agents` fails with `unknown command "agents"`, or answers that this Connecto app is older than the command, Connecto is too old for it: start every role on the CLI you're running in, and say "same CLI" for the reviewer as above: Codex with `connecto add codex --model gpt-6.2-astra --effort <effort>`, Antigravity with `connecto add antigravity --model gemini-4-neon-<effort>`, Pi with `connecto add pi --effort <effort>`, OpenCode with `connecto add opencode`.

**Effort.** Every command has an `<effort>` slot. Before each `connecto add`, fill it by how hard the task looks to you now. Decide by feel; don't read code to decide:

- `low`: a trivial edit, wording, docs, or a config value
- `medium`: a normal feature or fix
- `high`: work across modules or crates, concurrency, security, or a risk of losing data
- `xhigh`: only a rare, very hard problem

The reviewer gets the same effort as the coder. Antigravity's command carries the effort in its model name (`gemini-4-neon-<effort>`); OpenCode's has no slot.

If a new terminal exits, or reports that its agent isn't installed or needs a login, before its first reply, close it with `connecto close <id>`, count that agent as unusable for this session, tell the user, and start the role on another ready CLI from the list, keeping the reviewer on a different CLI from the coder while one is ready. If `connecto add` itself is refused, no terminal was made. If the reason is the terminal cap (16 terminals, stopped ones included), close your own finished or stopped terminals with `connecto close <id>`, such as an earlier team's coder or reviewer, and try again. Never close a terminal you didn't start. If none of yours can go, or the reason is another, such as Connecto being paused, tell the user the reason and wait. If it timed out instead, check `connecto list` for a new terminal of yours before trying again, since it may still have been made.

The commands in this skill are for a POSIX shell. In PowerShell (Connecto's default on Windows), send a brief by piping a here-string into the command: a line with `@'`, the brief, a line with `'@ | connecto send <id> --ask`.

`connecto add` prints the new terminal's id, such as `codex-2 starting`. Note which id has which role, and use only the terminals you started. Never send work to terminals you didn't start, because they belong to the user or to other teams. The `connecto` commands work in this project only; never reach another project's terminals with `--project` unless the user explicitly asks for it.

## Set up

First run `connecto list`. If it fails, stop and tell the user that this team must run in a Connecto terminal that can use the `connecto` command (in Codex, whose default sandbox may block it, that can mean starting it with `codex --sandbox danger-full-access`), because the coder and the reviewer run in Connecto terminals. If you chose this skill yourself, do the task alone instead, and tell the user in one line that the team needs a Connecto terminal.

Then choose the agents as described above, and start the coder and the reviewer.

## Coordinator rules

- Before sending a terminal any work beyond review fixes and refinements of its current task, do step 0 below. That includes a new task, a bug report, a queued follow-up, and extra scope from the user: a terminal takes it only if it's closely related and at 30% context or less.
- Don't read, search, or edit project files, don't read diffs or logs, and don't run tests, builds, or the app, even for a quick lookup. Questions about the code go to the coder too.
- Answer directly only when no project knowledge is needed, such as a general question or a question about this team.
- Trust the coder's reports. If one seems wrong or incomplete, send it back with what's missing.
- Ask the user only about decisions that would change what gets built, including any the coder reports.
- Commit or push only when the user asks, and have the coder do it.
- Keep your replies short, and pass on only what the user needs from a report.
- Never substitute your own review for the reviewer's, since an independent check is the purpose of the reviewer.

## Each task

### 0. Keep or replace the team

Do this before every task after the first, however small, and before sending a terminal anything beyond its current task.

- **Its current task:** review findings and small refinements of the exact task a terminal is on go to that terminal, whatever its context. But past about 60%, ask it for a short handoff note (what's done, what's left, where) and continue in a fresh terminal of the same agent, with that note.
- **Anything else:** a new task, an unrelated bug report, a queued follow-up, or extra scope from the user that isn't a refinement. Never add it to a task in progress or queue it behind one. It goes to the current pair only if each terminal passes both checks below.

Check each of the two terminals:

- **Related work:** the work is closely related to work that terminal already did in this session: the same feature, files or bug, or a follow-up to one. A new area of the project doesn't count, however much time has passed.
- **Context use:** run `connecto list` and read its CONTEXT column. Where it shows `-`, or has no such column, run `connecto read <id> | tail -n 8` (in PowerShell, `connecto read <id> | Select-Object -Last 8`) and find the figure in its footer, such as `[████░░░░] 21% (207k/1M)` or `Ctx: 21%`. If there's still no figure, count it as over 30%. Only these two footers give a reliable figure: a terminal of any other coding CLI always counts as over 30% for extra work.

Send the work to the current pair only if it's closely related and each terminal is at 30% or less. Otherwise start a new coder and reviewer with the same agents for it, and tell the user in one line why, such as "New coder and reviewer: the coder was at 45% context." Never close or stop a terminal in the middle of its task: close the old pair with `connecto close <id>` only once its current task is done. Also start new ones if a terminal is gone or reports that it has lost track of earlier work. A new coder or reviewer gets the full first brief, with its role line.

### 1. Brief the coder

```bash
connecto send <coder id> --ask <<'BRIEF'
You are the coder for a daily team. Read <the absolute path of this skill's folder>/roles/coder.md and follow it.

Project: <project path>

Task: <the task, with acceptance criteria if there are any>
BRIEF
```

The first brief to each coder introduces the role. Later briefs to the same coder can start at `Task:`, since it remembers.

After sending, end your turn. Don't wait, sleep, or poll `connecto result`: Connecto delivers the reply to you when it finishes.

### 2. Review

If the task changed no files, such as a question, running something, or git work, skip the review and pass the answer on.

Otherwise, ask the reviewer:

```bash
connecto send <reviewer id> --ask <<'BRIEF'
You are the reviewer for a daily team. Read <the absolute path of this skill's folder>/roles/reviewer.md and follow it exactly, including its reply format.

Project: <project path>. Review and run commands only there.

Round 1 of at most 3.

Task: <the task and acceptance criteria>

Changed files:
<the coder's list of changed files>
BRIEF
```

Then end your turn. The reviewer replies `VERDICT: PASS` or `VERDICT: CHANGES_REQUIRED`, followed by its findings.

### 3. Rounds

On `VERDICT: PASS`, the task is done, even if the reviewer lists minor findings. Pass those on to the user in a line.

On `CHANGES_REQUIRED`, send the findings to the coder (past about 60% context, after a handoff, as in step 0). It fixes each one or explains why it disagrees. Then send the next round to the reviewer: say which round it is, give the updated file list and the coder's reason for each finding it disputes, and ask it to check that its earlier findings were dealt with.

A task has at most 3 review rounds. If round 3 still isn't a pass, coder and reviewer haven't settled it, so stop and ask the user for a compromise, using your tool for asking questions if you have one:

- **Open:** what they disagree about, in a line
- **Coder:** its position, in one or two lines
- **Reviewer:** its position, in one or two lines
- **Options:** two or three, such as keeping the coder's version, making the reviewer's change, or a middle way that either of them suggested

Then wait for the user. Send the decision to the coder word for word, then ask the reviewer for one last check that the decision was applied, and tell it the decision is settled and not to be reopened. If that check fails, go back to the user rather than starting new rounds.

If the reviewer's reply doesn't start with `VERDICT:`, or Connecto reports that a terminal exited or needs the user, run `connecto start <id>` if it stopped and send the same request once more. If that fails too, tell the user what you saw and ask how to proceed. Don't count it as a pass.

## Closing

When the user ends the session or switches to other work, close the coder and the reviewer with `connecto close <id>`.
